unit: per job: one A/C condenser fitted, with the system evacuated and recharged. finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build, and it is HELD: only two of the four classes have a full labor range. Built totals (condenser + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2016 Mazda CX-3 about $449-$739 (1.9-2.0 hr); truck 2012 Silverado 1500 about $255-$688 (1.0-3.0 hr); midsize 2014 Chrysler 200 from about $328 (1.7 hr; no high, and it would be about $328-$591 if 1.7 hr were used at both ends); luxury 2015 Escalade no total (no hours). These totals leave out refrigerant, O-rings and compressor oil, which every job needs, and that is one reason they sit below the benchmarks ($600-$800 and $841-$988 are the tighter published bands; Jerry's $380-$1,360 is the widest); the other reasons are that the maker times are warranty times and the low parts figures are online prices. A supportable site range cannot be set until the midsize high and the luxury class are filled, but the evidence so far points to roughly $450-$1,000 for mainstream vehicles, more with R-1234yf refrigerant. How solid the labor times are: economy is the best, two Mazda warranty times printed with units, one for the CX-3 itself (1.2 hours to replace plus 0.7 hours to charge, added here) and one for a Mazda2 that uses the same condenser (2.0 Hrs including recharging); midsize has one Chrysler warranty time for the example vehicle (1.7 Hrs) that does not say whether it covers the recharge; the truck range is two parts-seller approximations (1 hour for an F-150, 3 hours for the Silverado), neither a book time and neither stating that the recharge is covered, so the truck low is probably the bolt-on swap alone and is thin; luxury has nothing usable. Many maker times were found but are cross-checks only: Honda's Civic, Accord Hybrid, Insight, Clarity and Civic Type R warranty extensions print the condenser replacement (1.1-1.6 hr; 2.7 hr on the Clarity) as a lettered line under a 1.0-1.7 hr leak-inspection operation, and the split between the two changed between versions of the Civic bulletin; Honda's Pilot/Ridgeline bulletin (2.2 hrs plus 0.7 hr recharge) includes replacing the filter sub-assembly; GM (3.3, later 0.8 plus recharge adds) and Subaru (0.4 plus 1.0) print no unit. Taken together the cross-checks put the whole job, with any inspection they include, at about 1.4 to 3.3 hours on most of these vehicles (4.4 hr on the Clarity plug-in hybrid), consistent with the ranges used. To finish: find a maker time with a unit, or a trade-press book time, for a luxury vehicle and a second one for a midsize vehicle, and verify a new aftermarket condenser for the luxury example. This is an estimate, never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote usually adds refrigerant (R-134a, or the much dearer R-1234yf on most cars built since the mid-2010s), new O-rings and compressor oil, leak diagnosis with dye or a sniffer, shop supplies and sales tax. Many shops replace the receiver-drier or desiccant whenever the system is opened, and on some vehicles it is built into the condenser. Vehicles with a front radar may need it aimed after the bumper or grille comes off (Honda lists 0.9-1.4 hr for that on its Pilot, Passport and Ridgeline). If the condenser failed from a front-end impact, the radiator, lines or supports may also be on the quote; if the compressor failed and sent debris through the system, the condenser is usually replaced as part of a much larger repair. Several makers have extended the condenser warranty on certain models (Honda Civic 2016-21 and others, Subaru Forester 2017-18, GM full-size SUVs 2015-17), so it is worth checking for coverage before paying.
